meta.headline: Can anything you say, sign or declare take you out of a court's power?
meta.seoTitle: Sovereign citizen courtroom tricks: what courts ruled

dek.text: Courts in the United States, Canada and New Zealand have rejected the idea that their power over you depends on your consent, and a declared status as a state citizen or a Moor has fared no better in the rulings reviewed here.

assertions.text: Courts in the United States, Canada and New Zealand have rejected the argument that a court has no jurisdiction without the person's consent.
Courts have rejected the claim that being a citizen of a state rather than of the United States removes federal court jurisdiction.
qualifications: The callout at s32 to s34 says these are federal tax cases and leave state jurisdiction untested.

assertions.text: A self-described Moor has no immunity from US law.

description.text: Courts have rejected the claim that their power needs your consent. What the rulings say about UCC 1-308, flag fringe and the act of 1871.

assertions.text: Courts in the United States, Canada and New Zealand have rejected the argument that a court has no jurisdiction without the person's consent.
UCC 1-308 concerns performance of a commercial contract during a dispute and does not address courts or criminal law.
The District government established by the act of 1871 was abolished by an act passed in 1874.

sections.name: hook
sections.heading: The defendant who told the judge he did not consent

sentences.text: An Ohio defendant opened his trial by declaring that he reserved his rights "per UCC 1-308 without prejudice" and that "I give the Court no consent".

assertions.text: In State v. Smith, an Ohio defendant told the court he reserved his rights "per UCC 1-308 without prejudice".

quote.text: per UCC 1-308 without prejudice

assertions.text: The same defendant told the court "I give the Court no consent".

quote.text: I give the Court no consent

sentences.text: The idea behind those words is that a court holds power over you only if you let it.
The idea is sold in several versions, and each leans on a real document: a section of the commercial code, the law of the flag, an old act of Congress, or the theory that statutes are contracts.
Below, each version is set against what its document actually says and what courts did when someone relied on it, followed by the related promise that declaring a new status puts you outside the law.

sections.name: question-1
sections.heading: Is there anything you can say, sign or point to that takes you out of a court's jurisdiction?

sentences.text: Promoters describe jurisdiction as something you hand over: the channel Out of Babylon says "there are various jurisdictions that do not have jurisdiction over you unless you grant them that jurisdiction".

assertions.text: Out of Babylon says "there are various jurisdictions that do not have jurisdiction over you unless you grant them that jurisdiction".

quote.text: there are various jurisdictions that do not have jurisdiction over you unless you grant them that jurisdiction
quote.speaker: Out of Babylon

sentences.text: To withhold it, The Grown Academy tells viewers to "write UCC 1-308 next to your signature All Rights Reserved".

assertions.text: The Grown Academy tells viewers to "write UCC 1-308 next to your signature All Rights Reserved".

quote.text: write UCC 1-308 next to your signature All Rights Reserved
quote.speaker: The Grown Academy

sentences.text: UCC 1-308 belongs to the Uniform Commercial Code, and its text protects a party that "performs, promises performance, or assents to performance" while expressly reserving its rights; "without prejudice" or "under protest" is enough wording to do that.

assertions.text: UCC 1-308 says a party that "performs, promises performance, or assents to performance" with an explicit reservation of rights does not prejudice the rights reserved, and "without prejudice" or "under protest" suffice.

quote.text: performs, promises performance, or assents to performance

sentences.text: The official comment gives the purpose as letting performance go on "along the lines contemplated by the contract despite a pending dispute", and the section says nothing about courts, police or criminal law.

assertions.text: The official comment says UCC 1-308 provides for the continuation of performance "along the lines contemplated by the contract despite a pending dispute".

quote.text: along the lines contemplated by the contract despite a pending dispute

assertions.text: UCC 1-308 concerns performance of a commercial contract during a dispute and does not address courts or criminal law.

sentences.text: The Ohio defendant was found guilty on all four charges, and the appeals court dealt with his code in a single line: "Any arguments related to the UCC are unavailing".

assertions.text: In State v. Smith the defendant was found guilty of all 4 charges, and the court noted "Any arguments related to the UCC are unavailing".

quote.text: Any arguments related to the UCC are unavailing

sentences.text: Refusing consent out loud has done no better than writing it down.

In United States v. Benabe, a federal appeals court held that whatever status a person claims, "that person is not beyond the jurisdiction of the courts", and that such theories "should be rejected summarily, however they are presented".

assertions.text: United States v. Benabe held that regardless of claimed status, "that person is not beyond the jurisdiction of the courts".

quote.text: that person is not beyond the jurisdiction of the courts
quote.speaker: United States v. Benabe

assertions.text: The Benabe court said these theories "should be rejected summarily, however they are presented".

quote.text: should be rejected summarily, however they are presented

sentences.text: Legal researchers Hobbs, Young and McIntyre describe three claimants who treated a court's authority as resting on their own consent; all three lost, and the authors give the reason: "no one needs to explicitly and affirmatively consent to the authority of a jurisdiction to be subject to it".

assertions.text: Hobbs, Young and McIntyre report 3 claimants who treated the court's authority as a matter of their consent; all 3 were unsuccessful.
Hobbs, Young and McIntyre write that "no one needs to explicitly and affirmatively consent to the authority of a jurisdiction to be subject to it".

quote.text: no one needs to explicitly and affirmatively consent to the authority of a jurisdiction to be subject to it

sentences.text: The flag version is stated in a letter to the Mountain Democrat: "The fringe denotes Admiralty law's jurisdiction".

assertions.text: A letter in the Mountain Democrat says "The fringe denotes Admiralty law's jurisdiction".

quote.text: The fringe denotes Admiralty law's jurisdiction
quote.speaker: Mountain Democrat

sentences.text: In McCann v. Greenway, a federal court that knew other courts had already called the argument frivolous examined the law of the flag anyway, "in the interest of killing this argument for good".

assertions.text: In McCann v. Greenway the court examined the law of the flag "in the interest of killing this argument for good", noting other courts had called it frivolous.

quote.text: in the interest of killing this argument for good

sentences.text: It quoted the Adjutant General of the Army, who wrote that a fringe "is not considered to be a part of the flag, and it is without heraldic significance".

assertions.text: McCann v. Greenway quotes the Adjutant General of the Army: a fringe "is not considered to be a part of the flag, and it is without heraldic significance".

quote.text: is not considered to be a part of the flag, and it is without heraldic significance
quote.speaker: Adjutant General

sentences.text: And it set out the rule that decides the question: "Jurisdiction is a matter of law, statute, and constitution, not a child's game wherein one's power is magnified or diminished by the display of some magic talisman".

assertions.text: McCann v. Greenway: "Jurisdiction is a matter of law, statute, and constitution, not a child's game wherein one's power is magnified or diminished by the display of some magic talisman".

quote.text: Jurisdiction is a matter of law, statute, and constitution, not a child's game wherein one's power is magnified or diminished by the display of some magic talisman

sentences.text: The 1871 version claims far more; the channel SYDLIS says "the act of 1871 that is exactly what changed america from a constitutional republic to a corporation".

assertions.text: SYDLIS says "the act of 1871 that is exactly what changed america from a constitutional republic to a corporation".

quote.text: the act of 1871 that is exactly what changed america from a constitutional republic to a corporation
quote.speaker: SYDLIS

sentences.text: The act is real, and in Metropolitan Railroad Co. v. District of Columbia the Supreme Court explained that it made the District of Columbia "a body corporate for municipal purposes", a local government able to make contracts and to sue and be sued.

assertions.text: The Supreme Court in Metropolitan R. Co. v. District of Columbia described the act of 1871 as constituting the District of Columbia "a body corporate for municipal purposes", with power to make contracts and sue and be sued, and a board of public works over its streets.

quote.text: a body corporate for municipal purposes

sentences.text: The Court called the District "a mere municipal corporation", said its sovereign power sits "in the government of the United States", and recorded that an act of 1874 abolished the government the 1871 act had created.

assertions.text: The Court held the District's character is that of "a mere municipal corporation".

quote.text: a mere municipal corporation

assertions.text: The Court said the sovereign power over the District is lodged "in the government of the United States".

quote.text: in the government of the United States

assertions.text: The District government established by the act of 1871 was abolished by an act passed in 1874.

sentences.text: The widest version treats every law as a private rulebook; Americans In Action says "these codes and statutes are only the bylaws of the corporation".

assertions.text: Americans In Action says "these codes and statutes are only the bylaws of the corporation".

quote.text: these codes and statutes are only the bylaws of the corporation
quote.speaker: Americans In Action

sentences.text: In Bey v. Indiana, when a man told the Seventh Circuit that Indiana could not tax him without a contract between them, the court answered "We have repeatedly rejected such claims".

assertions.text: In Bey v. Indiana the plaintiff argued he could not be taxed by Indiana absent a contract; the Seventh Circuit wrote "We have repeatedly rejected such claims".

quote.text: We have repeatedly rejected such claims
quote.speaker: Bey v. Indiana

sentences.text: In New Zealand, a self-described freeman-on-the-land who said he had never consented to the Land Transport Act had his claim struck out as an abuse of process; the researchers who reviewed the case note that "Everyone who operates a vehicle on public roads must comply with legislation regulating the operation of vehicles".

assertions.text: In James v The Corporation New Zealand Police, a freeman-on-the-land who said he had not consented to the Land Transport Act had his claim struck out as an abuse of process.
Hobbs, Young and McIntyre, on that case: "Everyone who operates a vehicle on public roads must comply with legislation regulating the operation of vehicles".

quote.text: Everyone who operates a vehicle on public roads must comply with legislation regulating the operation of vehicles

sentences.text: The record against the statutes-as-contracts argument here is a set of individual rulings, an American appeals court and a New Zealand case reported by researchers, rather than a count of every case; it shows the argument losing wherever it appears in this evidence, but it is not a census.

assertions.text: In Bey v. Indiana the plaintiff argued he could not be taxed by Indiana absent a contract; the Seventh Circuit wrote "We have repeatedly rejected such claims".
qualifications: s23 says the record is individual rulings, not a count.

assertions.text: In James v The Corporation New Zealand Police, a freeman-on-the-land who said he had not consented to the Land Transport Act had his claim struck out as an abuse of process.

sentences.text: So the answer is no: courts in the United States, Canada and New Zealand have each rejected the claim that a court's power over a person waits on that person's consent.

assertions.text: Courts in the United States, Canada and New Zealand have rejected the argument that a court has no jurisdiction without the person's consent.

sentences.text: How uniformly courts reject these arguments is best documented in Canada: Netolitzky and Warman report that no appeal built on them has been granted leave by the Supreme Court of Canada, and conclude "These ideas are pseudolaw, and devoid of merit".

assertions.text: Netolitzky and Warman report that to date no pseudolaw-based appeal has been granted leave by the Supreme Court of Canada, and write "These ideas are pseudolaw, and devoid of merit".

quote.text: These ideas are pseudolaw, and devoid of merit

qualifications: s25 limits this to Canada; s26 covers Australia and New Zealand and s27 the United States.

sentences.text: A review of cases from Australia and New Zealand reports that "No courts accept these arguments, and no courts absolve the claimant (or defendant) from their legal obligations and responsibilities".

assertions.text: Hobbs, Young and McIntyre write "No courts accept these arguments, and no courts absolve the claimant (or defendant) from their legal obligations and responsibilities".

quote.text: No courts accept these arguments, and no courts absolve the claimant (or defendant) from their legal obligations and responsibilities

qualifications: s26 names Australia and New Zealand as the review's scope.

sentences.text: For the United States this evidence holds no comparable count, only a run of rulings, which an Ohio appeals court summed up by saying such claims "continue to make their way to court and fail".

assertions.text: State v. Smith says this court and many others have repeatedly rejected such claims, which "continue to make their way to court and fail".

quote.text: continue to make their way to court and fail

qualifications: s27 says the US evidence is a run of rulings, not a count.

sections.name: question-2
sections.heading: Can declaring a different status, as a state national, a Moor or a free man, put me outside the law?

sentences.text: If no words in the courtroom work, promoters offer a new identity instead; Sovereign National describes citizenship as the status "which forces you into their statutes and codes and bylaws and we are not part of that".

assertions.text: Sovereign National says citizenship is what "which forces you into their statutes and codes and bylaws and we are not part of that".

quote.text: which forces you into their statutes and codes and bylaws and we are not part of that
quote.speaker: Sovereign National

sentences.text: Some sellers promise it works at the roadside too, with SPC University saying "when the officer runs your id he or she will see your status and has to let you go".

assertions.text: SPC University says "when the officer runs your id he or she will see your status and has to let you go".

quote.text: when the officer runs your id he or she will see your status and has to let you go
quote.speaker: SPC University

sentences.text: In federal statute, a national of the United States means "a citizen of the United States", or a non-citizen who owes the country permanent allegiance, so every citizen is already a national.

assertions.text: By statute, a national of the United States means "a citizen of the United States", or a non-citizen who owes permanent allegiance to the United States.

quote.text: a citizen of the United States

qualifications: The callout at s32 to s34 carries the limits of the court rulings on state citizenship.

sentences.text: The non-citizen kind of national status comes with birth, for instance in an outlying possession, not from a declaration a person files.

assertions.text: Every US citizen is a national of the United States, and non-citizen national status comes at birth, for example from birth in an outlying possession, not from a declaration.
qualifications: The callout at s32 to s34 carries the limits of the court rulings on state citizenship.

sentences.text: The court rulings here on declared state citizenship all come from federal tax litigation.

assertions.text: The federal rulings rejecting state-citizen status are from tax cases, so state jurisdiction is not covered.
qualifications: s32 and s34 state the tax-only scope.

sentences.text: In those cases federal appeals courts rejected the argument that being a citizen of a state rather than of the United States puts a person beyond the federal courts, and the Second Circuit called it "barely worth a footnote".

assertions.text: In tax cases, federal circuits rejected claims that being a citizen of a state rather than the United States puts a person beyond federal court jurisdiction; the Second Circuit called the argument "barely worth a footnote".

quote.text: barely worth a footnote

qualifications: s32 and s34 state the tax-only scope.

sentences.text: Because they are federal tax cases, they do not test whether the same declaration could take someone out of a state court's reach.

assertions.text: The federal rulings rejecting state-citizen status are from tax cases, so state jurisdiction is not covered.

sentences.text: The Moorish version rests on old treaties, and the Institute for Strategic Dialogue explains that "Moorish sovereigns cite that treaty to claim that Moors in the US have sovereign status, meaning they would be exempt from normal laws".

assertions.text: The Institute for Strategic Dialogue explains "Moorish sovereigns cite that treaty to claim that Moors in the US have sovereign status, meaning they would be exempt from normal laws".

quote.text: Moorish sovereigns cite that treaty to claim that Moors in the US have sovereign status, meaning they would be exempt from normal laws
quote.speaker: Institute for Strategic Dialogue

sentences.text: In Bey v. Indiana, a man who said that being a Moor made him a sovereign citizen asked the State of Indiana for an $11.5 billion refund.

assertions.text: In Bey v. Indiana, the plaintiff, who said being a Moor made him a sovereign citizen, sought an $11.5 billion refund from the State of Indiana.

blocks.caption: The refund the plaintiff in Bey v. Indiana asked for; the court dismissed the suit and awarded nothing.

sentences.text: The Seventh Circuit said the treaty argument is made "without any basis in fact" and that Bey "is a U.S. citizen and therefore unlike foreign diplomats has no immunity from U.S. law".

assertions.text: The Seventh Circuit said the argument that eighteenth-century treaties remove US jurisdiction over Moors is made "without any basis in fact".

assertions.text: The Seventh Circuit said Bey "is a U.S. citizen and therefore unlike foreign diplomats has no immunity from U.S. law".

sentences.text: The common-law version is taught by the National Liberty Alliance, which says "the un-codified common law is the superior law of the people and the codified civil law is the special or inferior law of the government".

assertions.text: The National Liberty Alliance says "the un-codified common law is the superior law of the people and the codified civil law is the special or inferior law of the government".

quote.text: the un-codified common law is the superior law of the people and the codified civil law is the special or inferior law of the government
quote.speaker: National Liberty Alliance

sentences.text: Magna Carta, often cited alongside it, had been repealed by 1969 except for three provisions, and in 1905 the High Court of Australia said the claim that a law is invalid for not conforming to it "is not one for serious refutation".

assertions.text: By 1969, the whole of Magna Carta save 3 provisions had been repealed.
In 1905 the High Court of Australia said the contention that a Commonwealth law is invalid for nonconformity with Magna Carta "is not one for serious refutation".

quote.text: is not one for serious refutation

sentences.text: Netolitzky and Warman report that the Supreme Court of Canada refused leave to applications relying on Magna Carta and historical English common law, which they read as an implicit rejection.

assertions.text: Netolitzky and Warman report that the Supreme Court of Canada denied leave in applications relying on Magna Carta and historical English common law, implicitly rejecting them.

sentences.text: Whether status papers protect a holder from being detained by police is a question this evidence cannot settle; the only source is an FBI bulletin reporting that three sovereign-citizen extremists in Kansas City were convicted for selling identification cards, at $450 to $2,000, that supposedly gave immunity from stops and arrests.

assertions.text: The FBI Law Enforcement Bulletin reports that 3 sovereign-citizen extremists in Kansas City were convicted for selling identification cards, at $450 to $2,000, that supposedly gave immunity from stops and arrests.
qualifications: s41 and s42 say the bulletin records the sellers' convictions, not what happened to holders at stops.

sentences.text: The bulletin records what happened to the sellers, not what happened to anyone who showed such a card at a stop.

assertions.text: The evidence on protection at stops is the one FBI report about sellers of immunity cards being convicted.

blocks.caption: The price range the convicted sellers charged for an ID card promising immunity from stops and arrests.

sentences.text: No court in this evidence accepted a declared status, whether citizenship of a state, Moorish nationality, or a free man's appeal to Magna Carta and the common law.

assertions.text: Courts have rejected the claim that being a citizen of a state rather than of the United States removes federal court jurisdiction.
qualifications: s32 and s34 say these rulings are federal tax cases.

assertions.text: A self-described Moor has no immunity from US law.
Courts have rejected the claim that Magna Carta or historical common law overrides statutes.

sections.name: close
sections.heading: Where a court's power comes from

sentences.text: Both answers rest on one rule: a court's power comes from law, statute and constitution, and no status a person claims puts them beyond it.

assertions.text: Jurisdiction is a matter of law, statute and constitution, not of displayed symbols.
Regardless of claimed status, a person is not beyond the jurisdiction of the courts.

sentences.text: Anyone offered a form, a code for the signature line or a card for the glovebox can ask the seller for a ruling where it worked, because the rulings where it was tried are public.
